paper_metadata.title: Benchmarking Highly Precise Quantum Linear Systems Algorithms

summary: The paper benchmarks HHL with iterative refinement for linear systems up to 8 variables, running on Quantinuum H2-2 hardware for 4-variable instances and on emulators/simulators for 8-variable cases. It reports that iterative refinement reduces solution error from about 0.8488 to 0.0008 on an 8-variable emulator case, while also enabling shallower circuits and fewer QPE qubits, but it does not demonstrate a practical classical-vs-quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Benchmarking HHL with iterative refinement (HHL-IR) for solving linear systems up to 8 variables on simulators/emulators and up to 4 variables on Quantinuum H2-2 hardware.

algorithm.convergence_criteria: Iterative refinement continues until residual norm satisfies the target tolerance ζ; quantum subroutine accuracy is controlled by fixed-precision OLS(ξ) in each refinement step.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Linear system Ax=b solved via HHL; QPE register used to estimate eigenvalues of A. No explicit qubit-to-variable encoding beyond the HHL state preparation and QPE registers is given.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Solve Ax = b and prepare a quantum state proportional to the solution vector |x⟩.

problem_instance.description: Hermitian linear systems of size up to 8 variables; hardware runs reported for a 4-variable unstructured system on Quantinuum H2-2 and emulator/simulator runs up to 8 variables.

dataset_specification.description: Unstructured linear systems; specific matrices not fully enumerated in the provided text.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: System normalized by α̃ = max(||A||F, ||b||); right-hand side normalized to b̃ and matrix to Ã.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Benchmarking across backends; comparison of solution error ||x_c - x_q|| and residual ||Ax-b|| across iterative refinement iterations and varying QPE register sizes.

noise_model.noise_type: hardware noise on NISQ device; noisy emulator/simulator also used

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Normalize A and b; compute residuals and scaling factors classically at each IR step.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Classical update x(k+1)=x(k)+η(k)^{-1}ũ(k) and residual recomputation.

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: Residuals and errors decrease across IR iterations; precision improves with more QPE qubits on small systems but can worsen on larger noisy runs due to noise accumulation.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: HHL without iterative refinement / direct high-precision QPE
speedup_claims.conditions: using iterative refinement with low-precision quantum solves; discussed for QLSAs on NISQ hardware
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper frames the improvement as in solution accuracy and resource reduction, not as a proven asymptotic runtime speedup over classical algorithms.
Reported for solution error reduction, from approximately 0.8488 to 0.0008.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: HHL-based QLSA with iterative refinement; asymptotic complexity not explicitly stated in the provided text.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: HHL with iterative refinement on Quantinuum H2-2 and emulators/simulators; reported up to 4-variable hardware runs and 8-variable emulator/simulator runs
limiting_factors: No classical solver baseline is reported for runtime or accuracy against the quantum method
Problem sizes are small (up to 4 variables on hardware)
The paper emphasizes resource reduction and improved precision, not end-to-end quantum advantage
HHL remains limited by QPE depth and noise on current hardware

notes: Hardware type is reported as Quantinuum H2-2, which is a gate-based trapped-ion QPU.

The paper reports QPE register size variation and system sizes up to 8 variables, but does not explicitly state total qubit counts or circuit depth in the provided text; these are therefore left null/inferred only at the experiment level.
Speedup order is not characterized asymptotically in the paper; only practical benchmarking and precision improvements are discussed.
The paper reports benchmarking and accuracy improvements from iterative refinement, but does not demonstrate quantum advantage over classical linear solvers.
The strongest quantitative result is an error reduction from approximately 0.8488 to 0.0008 on an 8-variable emulator case, i.e. over 3 orders of magnitude improvement relative to HHL without IR.
